title: Chapter 21 — Going Aboard
paragraphs: It was nearly six o'clock, but only a gray, imperfect, misty dawn when we approached the wharf.
"There are some sailors running ahead there, if I'm seeing right," said I to Queequeg. "Those can't be shadows. She must be leaving by sunrise, I think. Come on!"

"Stop!" cried a voice. Its owner came up close behind us, laid a hand on both our shoulders, and then pushed himself between us. Stooping forward slightly in the uncertain twilight, he peered strangely from Queequeg to me. It was Elijah.
"Going aboard?"
"Hands off, will you," said I.
"Look here," said Queequeg, shaking himself free, "go away!"
"Not going aboard, then?"
"Yes, we are," said I, "but what business is that of yours? Do you know, Mr. Elijah, that I consider you rather rude?"
"No, no, no — I wasn't aware of that," said Elijah, slowly looking from me to Queequeg and back with the strangest glances.
"Elijah," said I, "you would do my friend and me a favor by going away. We're heading to the Indian and Pacific Oceans and would prefer not to be delayed."
"Are you, are you? Coming back before breakfast?"
"He's crazy, Queequeg," said I. "Come on."
"Hello there!" cried Elijah, calling after us when we had gone a few steps.
"Ignore him," said I. "Queequeg, come on."
But he crept up to us again and, suddenly clapping his hand on my shoulder, said, "Did you see anything that looked like men heading toward that ship a little while ago?"
Struck by this straightforward, matter-of-fact question, I answered, "Yes, I thought I saw four or five men, but it was too dim to be sure."
"Very dim, very dim," said Elijah. "Morning to you."
Once more we left him behind. But once more he came softly after us, and touching my shoulder again, said, "See if you can find them now, will you?"
"Find who?"

"Morning to you! Morning to you!" he called back, moving off again. "Oh! I was going to warn you against — but never mind, never mind — it's all one, all in the family too. Sharp frost this morning, isn't it? Goodbye to you. Won't be seeing you again very soon, I guess — unless it's before the Grand Jury." And with those wild words he finally departed, leaving me for the moment in no small amazement at his frantic boldness.

At last, stepping aboard the Pequod, we found everything in deep quiet. Not a soul was moving. The cabin entrance was locked from inside. The hatches were all closed and piled with coils of rigging. Going forward to the forecastle, we found the scuttle slide open. Seeing a light, we went down and found only an old rigger there, wrapped in a tattered jacket. He was stretched out full length across two sea chests, face down, his head buried in his folded arms. The deepest sleep had taken hold of him.

"Those sailors we saw, Queequeg — where could they have gone?" said I, looking doubtfully at the sleeper. But it seemed that Queequeg hadn't noticed what I was referring to when we were on the wharf. I would have thought I was seeing things, if not for Elijah's otherwise inexplicable question. But I pushed the thought aside. Looking again at the sleeper, I jokingly suggested to Queequeg that perhaps we should sit up with the body, and told him to make himself comfortable. He put his hand on the sleeper's rear end, as if testing whether it was soft enough, and then, without further hesitation, sat right down on it.
"Good Lord! Queequeg, don't sit there," said I.
"Oh! Very good seat," said Queequeg. "My country way. Won't hurt him face."

"Face!" said I. "You call that his face? A very friendly-looking face, then. But listen to how hard he's breathing — he's heaving up and down. Get off, Queequeg, you're heavy. You're crushing the poor man's face. Get off, Queequeg! Look, he'll throw you off any second. I'm amazed he doesn't wake up."

Queequeg moved himself just past the sleeper's head and lit his tomahawk pipe. I sat at the feet. We passed the pipe back and forth over the sleeper between us. Meanwhile, when I questioned him in his broken way, Queequeg explained that in his land, due to the complete lack of benches and sofas, the king, chiefs, and important people had the custom of fattening some of the lower classes to use as furniture. To furnish a house comfortably, you only had to buy eight or ten lazy fellows and scatter them around the rooms. Besides, they were very convenient on outings — much better than those garden chairs that fold into walking sticks. On occasion, a chief would simply call his attendant and order him to make himself into a bench under a spreading tree, perhaps in some damp marshy spot.
While telling these stories, every time Queequeg took the tomahawk from me, he flourished the hatchet end of it over the sleeper's head.
"What's that for, Queequeg?"
"Very easy, kill him. Oh! Very easy!"

He was going on with some wild memories about his tomahawk-pipe, which had apparently both brained his enemies and soothed his soul, when we were suddenly drawn to the sleeping rigger. The thick smoke had completely filled the cramped space and was starting to affect him. He breathed with a sort of muffled sound, then seemed bothered in his nose, then rolled over once or twice, then sat up and rubbed his eyes.
"Hey there!" he finally wheezed. "Who are you smokers?"
"Signed-on crew," I answered. "When does she sail?"
"Oh, you're going on her, are you? She sails today. The captain came aboard last night."
"What captain — Ahab?"
"Who else?"
I was about to ask him more questions about Ahab when we heard noise on deck.

"Hey! Starbuck's up and about," said the rigger. "He's a sharp chief mate, that one — good man and religious. But he's fully awake now, so I've got to get to work." And with that he went up on deck, and we followed.

It was now clear sunrise. Soon the crew came aboard in twos and threes. The riggers got to work. The mates were busy giving orders. And several people from shore were bringing various last things on board. Meanwhile, Captain Ahab remained invisibly shut away inside his cabin.
